podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: How does Universal Music Group identify and capitalize on unreleased tracks trending on TikTok before official release?
transcript_excerpt: Universal first looks at what is working and identifies gaps using competitive tools to see what fits the mold and what is not filled. When something is building user-generated content, they keep pumping that phase. Once it connects and people are talking about the song in comments, they shift to tastemaker content like simple carousels connecting the trend to the artist itself, then use AI tools and individual thought to identify which niche of TikTok or other platforms the audience lives on and what content is missing.

podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: Why do viral meme songs on TikTok often fail to translate into streaming growth for artists?
transcript_excerpt: Songs that go viral as memes can get hundreds of thousands of user-generated content with A-list celebrities using them, but because they are just for the meme and not focused around the song itself, they do not necessarily translate to streaming. Danny notes these viral moments can negatively impact an artist by inflating numbers where they should not be inflated, and they often just do nothing for streaming.

podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: What are the top KPIs Universal Music Group tracks to measure music marketing success beyond follower counts?
transcript_excerpt: The two biggest KPIs are streaming growth and follower growth. Third to that is Google Trends data, which shows whether people are actually searching for an artist or even specific lyrics from their songs. This reveals if something meaningful is happening that should be capitalized on, even when viral follower growth and streaming numbers are not immediately visible.

podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: How does Universal Music Group work with artists like Adele and Florence and the Machine who resist active social media participation?
transcript_excerpt: Danny emphasizes that labels cannot make artists do anything they do not want to do, and artists generally have full autonomy over their socials. Instead of forcing participation, Universal uses a creator strategy focused on clipping rich archives of existing content—interview clips, behind-the-scenes moments, TV appearances—that can be seeded repeatedly so artists can focus on making music and playing live while the label handles social amplification.

podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: Why does Universal Music Group prioritize targeting children aged 7-13 for initial fandom building despite regulatory restrictions?
transcript_excerpt: Initial fandom comes from around 7 or 8 years old up to 13—the artists you love during that period stay with you forever. Once you reach mid-twenties, your relationship with new artists becomes passive and they may only be loved for a few years. YouTube is key for this because you can target younger audiences watching on connected TV with their parents through gaming channels and toy unboxing content, which is not available on TikTok or Instagram to the same degree.

podcast_name: SocialMinds - A Social Media Marketing Podcast
episode_title: Universal Music Group on the difference between going viral and building a fanbase | Danny Ingram, Director of Creator Marketing
question: How does Universal Music Group treat catalog tracks that resurface through film and television placements versus new song releases?
transcript_excerpt: Catalog songs can become top hits through sync placements—for example, Go by Chemical Brothers became a top five hit after Taron Edgerton used it in a hunting scene. When songs are tied to emotional moments or beloved actors in scenes, they become stickier than official release placements. Universal also keeps calendar reminders on evergreen songs like Heat Waves by Glass Animals, which has a lyric mentioning June, so they prep content around that time knowing it will translate to streaming every year.
